rules.concept: transitivity of verb uses and dual-transitivity verbs
rules.statement: Transitivity classifies both clauses and particular uses of verbs: a dual-transitivity verb has one use with an object and another without one.
rules.condition: When classifying a canonical clause by its internal core complements, determine whether that particular use of the verb has an object; do not assume that every use of a lexeme has the same transitivity.

contrast.text: Mira read quietly. [intransitive use of read]
Mira read the instructions. [transitive use of read]
The window opened. [intransitive use of open]
Nia opened the window. [transitive use of open]

rules.review_notes: The section names verbs that occur both with and without an object as dual-transitivity verbs. This refines, rather than replaces, the existing COMP-002 treatment of verb subclasses. Explicitly approved by the repository owner on 2026-11-05.

rules.statement: Core complements are prototypically NPs related directly to the verb, whereas non-core complements are prototypically PPs that relate their NP to the verb through a preposition.
rules.condition: When describing the prototypical form and relation of a verb complement in clause structure, distinguish direct NP core complements from PP non-core complements; the distinction is a prototype, not an exceptionless form requirement.

exceptions.description: The NP/PP pattern is prototypical rather than exhaustive: core predicative complements can also be realised by AdjPs as well as NPs.

contrast.text: Ravi sent Mira the parcel. [the subject and both object NPs are core complements]
Ravi sent the parcel to Mira. [to Mira is a non-core PP complement]
The visitors seemed remarkably patient. [AdjP predicative complement; core complement beyond the NP prototype]
contrast.note: Tests the stated restriction on the NP prototype.

rules.statement: An oblique is an NP related to the verb indirectly through a preposition, rather than directly as a core NP complement.
rules.condition: When an NP occurs inside a PP that functions as a complement of the verb, classify the PP as the verb's complement and the NP inside that PP as an oblique.

contrast.text: Ava gave Leo a book. [Leo is an NP core complement]
Ava gave a book to Leo. [to Leo is a PP complement; Leo is its oblique]

rules.statement: The predicand of a predicative complement is the entity to which that complement attributes a property; it may be the clause subject or an object, and it is not thereby the syntactic subject of the predicative complement.
rules.condition: In a clause containing a predicative complement, identify the NP or pronoun of which the predicative complement makes a predication; label that constituent the predicand whether it functions as subject or object of the governing verb.

contrast.text: Noah seemed calm. [Noah is subject of seemed and predicand of calm]
The coach considered Noah calm. [Noah is object of considered and predicand of calm]

rules.statement: Predicative complements are normally subject-oriented in complex-intransitive clauses and object-oriented in complex-transitive clauses; in a passive counterpart, an object-oriented predicative complement is re-oriented to the subject.
rules.condition: When a predicative complement occurs in a complex-intransitive or complex-transitive construction, determine its orientation by the predicand; in a passive counterpart of a complex-transitive clause, the predicand becomes subject and the predicative complement is subject-oriented.

contrast.text: Elena seemed calm. [subject-oriented predicative complement]
The panel considered Elena calm. [object-oriented predicative complement]
Elena was considered calm. [passive; predicative complement re-oriented to subject]

rules.concept: predicative complement construction versus finite clause complement construction
rules.statement: A clause with a predicative complement and a corresponding construction with a finite subordinate clause are syntactically distinct, even when they convey closely related predications.
rules.condition: When comparing a matrix verb's predicative-complement pattern with a finite-clause pattern, distinguish the predicative complement directly licensed in the first construction from the subordinate clause functioning as complement in the second.

contrast.text: Rae seemed nervous. [predicative complement construction]
It seemed that Rae was nervous. [finite subordinate clause complement]
Rae considered Malik reliable. [predicative complement construction]
Rae considered that Malik was reliable. [finite subordinate clause complement]

rules.statement: In this chapter's terminology, a copular clause is the common complex-intransitive construction with be as predicator and a predicative complement.
rules.condition: When a complex-intransitive clause has be as its predicator and a predicative complement related to its subject, classify it as a copular clause under the terminology adopted in this chapter.

exceptions.description: Although some usage applies 'copular' more broadly to complex-intransitive constructions with verbs other than be, this chapter reserves the term for the be construction and uses complex-intransitive for the broader pattern.

contrast.text: Sam was exhausted. [copular clause: be as predicator]
Sam became exhausted. [complex-intransitive, but not called copular under this chapter's narrower terminology]
contrast.note: Tests the chapter's restriction of the term copular.

rules.statement: In this chapter, valency classifies a verb by the number of syntactic complements it combines with: one, two, three, or four complements correspond to monovalent, bivalent, trivalent, and quadrivalent patterns.
rules.condition: When assigning valency in this chapter's sense, count the clause's syntactic complements, including the subject and any internal complements, without using transitivity alone as the count.

contrast.text: Mia slept. [monovalent: one complement, the subject]
The price depends on the supplier. [bivalent: subject and PP complement]
Owen sent Mira a parcel. [trivalent: subject and two object complements]
I bet you ten dollars that the train will be late. [quadrivalent: subject and three further complements]
